en: The Collected Poems of King Fanzhi. Preface: [Omitted].

His Majesty, relying solely upon the Buddhist teachings and the Way of the Dharma—namely non-self, suffering, and emptiness—has understood the karmic conditions of past meager merit and the causes and effects of the future.
He has compiled these works to encourage virtue and admonish against transgressions. Although the table of contents consists of but a few...
He composed over three hundred poems in various styles,
all of which addressed contemporary affairs without being frivolous or hollow.
He discussed the noble writings of Wang Fanzhi and practiced the essential meanings of Ding and Guo;
he did not accept the canonical scriptures, instead employing only common vernacular speech.
Not only is it easy for the wise to turn their minds,
but even the common folk can change their countenances;
as this report spreads far and near, they are exhorted and summoned to cultivate goodness.
Those with greedy histories have encroached and plundered;
officials who merely draw their stipends ought to be upright and prudent.
Though each of us is ignorant, our feelings are profoundly sorrowful.
To seek [the meaning] once in brief, to contemplate it three times, and to never forget it—
were even a Great Virtue to lecture upon this,
it would not equal the merit of reading these excellent writings.
A disobedient son who merely performs the formal visits of morning and evening turns such "filial piety" into its opposite;
a lazy wife who neglects her service to her parents-in-law every morning and evening causes even the sons of Master Cha to feel shame.
Travelers from various provinces yearn for their hometowns;
the indolent man rises at night,
and the lazy woman stays awake until dawn.
All have gathered before the silken baskets;
knowing both sin and merit, they plow with diligence and toil until their mouths are satisfied.
Their single resolve and five emotions remain unchanged.
From the eastern provinces to the western commanderies, all alike praise it;
simply by becoming thoroughly familiar with this chapter, even the stubborn,
the foolish, the ignorant, and the dull-witted shall all become wise and virtuous.
Gazing afar at the people of the world,
in villages, hamlets, and settlements,
within each single household there is both death and birth.
The entire village gathered together and wept;
they cried out at the corpses of others,
unaware that their own departure was imminent.
Originally a ghost of eternal slumber,
now briefly standing upon the earth;
it is like a woolen rug for nursing a child.
Turning from the dry, one follows the moist;
having deeply understood the principle of the former death,
one enters upon the continuity of the latter death.
"When I was wealthy and possessed money,
my wife and children looked upon me with favor;
but when I stripped off my clothes,"
"Give me my layered robe and tunic;
I am going out to seek the scriptures.
Send me off, and I shall immediately set out upon the road."
As he was about to enter the house,
he saw my face full of smiles;
white doves circled around me.
Pitied like a parrot,
meeting with poverty for a brief moment;
look at me and you will see my face is haggard.
A person has seven states of poverty and seven forms of wealth;
these four signs are retributions for past deeds.
To pursue wealth while disregarding people [is a mark of poverty].
Furthermore, look at what was said when he arrived:
"My family and dependents have all perished;
when I die, I shall have no relatives or kinsmen."
Hastily purchase assets and establish offerings;
perform preparatory rites and vegetarian feasts so that one may be reborn in a favorable place.
When the body dies, hire someone to bury it;
let the neighbors and guarantors pay for the expenses;
you may arrange matters as you see fit.
The body is like a sheep within a pen;
the retribution of its life is exactly appropriate.
The sheep immediately shatters its wool and flees.
A person dressed in fine garments,
upon stripping off the clothes and standing naked,
is then no better than a sheep.
The sheep died day after day;
the people likewise perished day after day,
being seized by the head and led away.
It is just like a fat, healthy sheep;
the sheep dies in bitter suffering,
yet when the person departs, there is no brokenness or injury left behind.
When life ends and one flees elsewhere,
the soul wanders through foreign lands;
if one possesses wealth, one can perform much merit.
Wearing fine clothes,
the fool commits many sins;
the wise person reflects well.
How laughable are the people of this world!
They are full of folly and possess little wisdom;
they do not worry that the road to death is long.
Attached to the afflictions of suffering,
they sleep at night and wander through the realm of ghosts;
when dawn breaks, they return to the human path.
Suddenly they rise up, seizing and dragging one another, wailing and crying out for relief;
having no place to escape their poverty and suffering,
they are joined together and subjected to whipping and torture.
There is suffering at the time of birth;
it would be better to die early.
Others laugh at my poverty; I am poor.
I am extremely happy in my poverty;
having neither ox nor horse,
I do not worry about being plundered by the lowly.
You, a wealthy householder, have high status;
you employ both shame and profit.
I have no place for such summoning.
Eating to satiety with legs stretched out long;
you, wealthy one, wear a brocade robe.
Yet you are constantly bound and fettered.
Though impoverished and suffering, he has no afflictions;
wearing grass garments upon his body,
he is a truly great and deluded lord.
He was a widower with no sons;
he greedily sought great wealth and maintained many male and female slaves.
The Lord of Death calls at the gate;
there is no guest-farewell with neighbors.
When death arrives, one receives only four wooden planks.
A single yellow shroud for the body;
wealth and slaves are for use.
One may employ them as one sees fit in other enterprises.
Having wealth but not knowing how to use it is like entering the capital empty-handed.
This is the general principle of the Way.
Bearing the ghost of ignorance,
one dies suddenly in a state of frantic agitation;
immediately, the messengers of the Lord of Death search everywhere for them.
Bound back-to-back with a staff,
they crossed the Nai River and were carried face-down to the front of the hall.
Fetters and clubs rise up all over their bodies;
they die after seven days and undergo punishment as ox-demons.
The head is struck by the money-fork, and the feet are seized;
the body is pounded by the pestle and ground by the millstone.
Reborn again and again, one dies once more.
Chaos and confusion cause the loss of essence;
there is no way to see within the home.
The wife is the child, yet she is made a servant by another after her husband has passed away.
The slave serves the new lord;
the maid follows the lady.
Four horses are fitted with golden saddles.
The lamp-stands are carved with intricate patterns,
the silver bits and reins gleam; the horn-bow lacks a master,
and the precious sword lies prostrate upon the ground.
If you set aside these hundred days,
your entire family will forget you;
the wealth will be used by others.
This has been the common way since antiquity:
those who came before hoarded and accumulated,
while those who followed felt no shame or remorse.
This is a slave guarding wealth;
failing to exchange it, he dies in poverty.
Husband and wife sit facing one another.
A thousand years would not be enough;
one person lies ill upon their bed.
Looking from afar, the hand cannot touch; when the heart’s retribution arrives at the end, it is too late.
In vain one expends wealth;
treasures accumulate like mountains,
yet at death one receives but a single coffin.
Empty-handed, he grasps two fists;
in his mouth he vainly holds jade.
He shall forever part from the mirror upon the dais.
Without mind, when opening one's clothes, dust fills every pore;
the scissors produce the robe [at the seam].
This is the place for sitting upright and performing song and dance.
There is no way to practice melodies further;
the lute has lost its resonant laughter,
and the strings of the zither are snapped and will not join again.
The flowers cause the eyes of later generations to grieve;
it is because those who came before lacked merit that they were born in the Hall of Seven Jewels.
Upon death, one enters the earth and encounters the touch of the corner [of the coffin];
the funeral carriages hook and pull against one another;
and the ghosts return to wail for each other.
Every day, thousands of things are buried;
light and shadow pass with such rapidity.
The wealthy prepare their coffins.
In the corner of a poor man’s mat,
we sing together "What can be done?
As we send you off to an empty grave.
When the thousand cease, the ten thousand cease;
forever parting from the pleasures of this life,
those with resolve enter the Western Land.
Fools fall into hell; with their heads downward, they enter the sea of suffering,
remaining in darkness without awakening.
Carrying one's head high as one walks through the village;
when the occasion arises, one should display one's boots and robes.
If one has money, simply spend it as one pleases.
Do not practice the "thousand-year ruse.
In a hundred years, there may be but one person;
those who reach seventy are rare.
With eyes wide open, one watches them die,
unable to awaken to this oneself;
a skin of folly envelops pus and blood.
Stubborn bones follow one another;
with two feet walking like a clothes rack, step by step toward Avīci.
A pair of blind ones who do not recognize ghosts.
The Lord of Death hastens to pursue him;
a red cord is tied around his neck,
and he is bound crosswise with a staff through his back skin.
Walking with head bared and feet bare,
with no clothing upon the body,
one’s heart alone races within.
Surrounded on all four sides by troops,
ten taxations lie ahead,
and iron hammers strike from behind.
The Lord of Death draws his bow and shoots;
the agony is more intense than knives or needles.
The messengers call from the gate; one is filled with panic, for there is no time to delay.
Naked, they were driven away;
the entire household wailed in grief together.
The house was left without its protector.
The wife and children are deceived by others;
wealth and property are no longer one's own.
The estate is gathered and forever departed.
The three *hún* souls have no place to rest;
the seven *pò* spirits scatter and fly from the head.
One drifts and sinks into the three evil realms.
No one in the household knows [of this].
Having clothes, one cannot wear them;
having horses, one cannot ride them.
There are slaves one cannot command;
there are maidservants who do not follow;
there is food one cannot eat.
In the past, one constantly suffered from hunger; now,
in the dark depths of hell, there is suffering,
and it is difficult to see the time of emergence.
□ Proceeding one after another, he returns to life; who is it that knows this?
He skillfully exhorts the nobles and others.
By constructing bridges to ferry others across, one gains the merit of being reborn in the Western Pure Land; by knowing contentment, one realizes that the body is finite.
The journey of this body is far too arduous.

Yet, one merely gives rein to [the senses], and as the candle-flame turns, people are driven to madness; they buy brocade for their wives while remaining heartless themselves, falling into error through such delusions.
One can only endure temporary toil;
one’s life is wasted entering into bitter suffering.
Looking on from the side... [they] construct houses and dwellings.
In ten thousand years, there is but one person who attains it.
Even if one were to live for a long period of a hundred years, it would be like the fleeting light of a star for but a moment.

In the midst of this, life is as brief as a child’s play; whether it be a man or a woman, do not be startled or anxious. Examine the three realms: the months of darkness increase, harming the body and flesh; day by day one commits sins, never knowing contentment.
Deng Qingzhang, Academician of the Great Yun Temple.
